findings.element: the day's own editor (.b-edit, theDay branch) and the horizon it feeds (.b-num / .b-unit / .b-when / .b-sub)
findings.problem: theDayRecord() (render-b.js:163) identifies the day by matching a milestone's date against F.project.primaryDate.date, and setAway() (render-b.js:727) writes record.date without ever writing F.project.primaryDate.date. So one press of a stepper in the day's own editor severs the day from the project, and every string built on that identity goes false while staying on screen. Driven at 1440 on ?v=paper&state=owner-flight, opening the row aria-labelled 'Edit Wedding day' (the editor names itself 'Editing the day itself' and carries the standing note 'Everything on this plan is measured from this day'), then one press of the minus-one stepper: the row becomes 'Wedding day / Fri 2 Oct', the undo bar says 'Wedding day moved 1 day earlier.', and the horizon four hundred pixels away still reads '79 / days / Saturday 3 October 2026 / Wedding day' - the largest type on the surface naming a date the plan no longer contains. Three further strings fall with it. (a) Reopening that row now says 'Editing Wedding day', not 'Editing the day itself', and the panel now offers 'Shown / Hidden' and 'Delete this moment' on the day itself - the exact controls render-b.js:1065 exists to withhold ('Hiding it would hide the thing every figure on the page is measured from'). (b) Renaming it now leaves the horizon on the old name: setTitle()'s isTheDay branch (render-b.js:866), written precisely so 'the row and the horizon carry two names for one day' cannot happen, no longer fires - measured 'Our wedding' on the row and in the undo bar against 'Wedding day' on the horizon in the same frame. (c) The ceiling is still computed from F.project.primaryDate.date, so with the day on 2 October another moment can be typed to 3 October and is accepted with no refusal, landing last in the measure, while the sentence the same field prints one press earlier still says 'Nothing can sit after the day itself.' The same sequence with no prior move renames correctly, which is what isolates the date-match as the cause.
findings.fix: Give the day a stable identity and one writer. In fixture.js add milestoneId: "demo-audience-item-wedding" to PROJECT.primaryDate, and rewrite theDayRecord() to return recordFor(F.project.primaryDate.milestoneId) || F.milestones.filter(function (m) { return m.date === F.project.primaryDate.date; })[0] || null, so identity survives a move. Then in setAway(), after 'if (record) record.date = iso;', add 'if (isTheDay(record)) { F.project.primaryDate.date = iso; repaintHorizon(root); }'. repaintHorizon(root) is a four-line writer beside setTitle's existing branch: rewrite .b-num to String(F.days(clock, F.project.primaryDate.date)), .b-unit through countBlock's own unit rule, .b-when to F.fmt.longYear(F.project.primaryDate.date) and .b-sub to F.project.primaryDate.label. Because setAway clamps to ceiling = daysFrom(clock, F.project.primaryDate.date), compute ceiling before the write and skip the clamp when isTheDay(record) is true, so the day may move later as well as earlier; the undo closure already restores the old away value and will now restore the horizon through the same call.

findings.problem: The two largest figures on the publish screen disagree by a day, and the caption between them is what makes the disagreement legible. card() (render-b.js:1831) builds the figure from F.toDay() - the distance from today - and captions it 'days away when this was sent', a phrase whose own comment says it exists so 'the card has to be true a month later'. pressHead() on the same screen builds its headline from F.publication.publishedAt and prints 'Mara & Finn have had this since 15 July.' Measured in the page: F.today 2026-07-16, F.publication.publishedAt 2026-07-15, F.days(publishedAt, weddingDate) = 80, F.days(today, weddingDate) = 79, .b-ogNum = '79'. So the card asserts it was 79 days away when it was sent and the headline beside it asserts it was sent on a day when it was 80. The same one-day error is baked into the card's accessible name ('Mara & Finn, 79 days away when this was sent...') and into state=unfurl, which is the card as it actually landed in the message - the code's own 'first impression inside a message'. Two accessors for one fact, on the one screen where the product asks to be trusted with a link. The behaviour gate never catches it: interaction-check.mjs:3673-3676 tests only that the string 'when this was sent' is present, never that the figure beside it is measured from the send.
findings.fix: One accessor. In card() replace 'var said = F.countdown(F.toDay());' with 'var sent = F.publication.publishedAt ? F.publication.publishedAt.slice(0, 10) : null; var said = F.countdown(F.days(sent || F.today, F.project.primaryDate.date));' and gate the caption on the same value: where sent is set keep said.unit + " away when this was sent", and where it is null - nothing published yet, the branch where pressHead returns 'Send it to Mara & Finn.' - print said.unit + " away", so the preview does not claim a send that has not happened. figureSaid is built from the same two variables and follows automatically.

findings.problem: The printed sheet dates itself in one place and speaks deixis in the other, and the file already states the rule it breaks. countBlock() sets the print unit to 'days away on Thursday 16 July 2026' under a comment reading 'Paper cannot be reloaded, so it dates itself', and horizon() drops .b-todayLabel on print under a comment reading 'Today is a screen fact.' Both are right. But the rail origin two hundred pixels away still prints 'Today, 16 July' (render-b.js:215), which is false the moment the sheet leaves the printer - and this is the keepsake, the artifact that exists to be read on the morning and kept afterwards. The mark also speaks a grammar no other mark on its own rail speaks: measured on state=print, every row date is weekdayShort + short ('Sat 1 Aug', 'Sat 8 Aug', 'Sat 3 Oct') while the zero mark of the same rail reads 'Today, 16 July'. So the sheet carries three grammars for two facts where two of them are already correct.
findings.fix: In measure(), make the origin's text medium-aware: text: o.medium === "print" ? F.fmt.weekdayShort(clock) + " " + F.fmt.short(clock) : "Today, " + F.fmt.medium(clock). On paper the zero mark then reads 'Thu 16 Jul' - the grammar every other mark on that rail already speaks, anchoring the rail without claiming a day the reader is not in - and on every screen medium the line is unchanged.

findings.problem: The first sentence a new owner ever reads calls the thing by a name the product uses nowhere else. 'Everything on this page is measured from it, so it is the only thing needed to start.' is the only visible string in the master that calls the object a page; every other one calls it the plan - 'Back to the plan', 'The plan as guests will see it.', 'The plan stays online at', 'The plan has not been deleted', 'It carries the day, the distance and the plan', 'This is the day the plan was for.' - and the accessible name of the very section this sentence sits inside is 'The plan for Aisling & Tom'. Its own twin says the other word: the day's editor prints 'Everything on this plan is measured from this day.', the same sentence-shape stating the same law with the product's noun in it. 'Page' is a browser's word, not this product's, and it lands on the reader the brief describes as never having used a tool like this, at the one moment the product is teaching them what it is.
findings.fix: render-b.js:1695 - change 'Everything on this page is measured from it, so it is the only thing needed to start.' to 'Everything on this plan is measured from it, so it is the only thing needed to start.'

biggestWin: The document has one voice and it holds under pressure. Every refusal states the rule and then names what still stands - 'That is not a date. Try 3 October 2026.', 'That day has gone. Pick one still ahead.', 'This is as near as it goes. Tomorrow is the soonest.' - declarative, sentence case, no apology, no exclamation, nothing a person has to be taught. The plural lives in one function, the countdown answers with a state rather than a string so the morning gets 'Today' at display size and the day after gets a sentence with no numeral in it, and the keepsake changes its own unit line to date the figure because paper cannot be reloaded. Nothing anywhere reads as filler. And the palette is spent rather than obeyed: indigo is two marks and a line - the rule under today, the filled tick on the next thing, the rail that is still ahead - and it survives the ground flip intact, so the ink room is the same room at night and not a theme laid over it. Set beside Linear or Stripe this reads as writing somebody argued about, which is the rarest thing on this list.
